title: St. Francis Dam Disaster
draftNote: Draft by Claude, 5 October 2026, read-only research for Nathan. Nothing written to Craft. Sources read from the local index of the Reggie mirror built earlier this session (the drive was not mounted today), and from Craft by read-only queries. Nothing from Wikipedia or general knowledge.

fields.eventSignificance: The St. Francis Dam in San Francisquito Canyon failed on the night of March 12, 1928, and its flood ran 54 miles to the sea, killing an estimated 411 people. In this valley it destroyed Powerhouse No. 2 and the homes around it, ranches in the canyon, and nearly everything at Castaic Junction.
fields.body:
The St. Francis Dam stood at the head of San Francisquito Canyon, above Saugus. The City of Los Angeles had completed it about two years before, under its chief engineer, William Mulholland, to store an emergency water supply.[1][2] It failed in the last minutes of March 12, 1928: at 11:57:30 p.m. by Leon Worden's captions, "on or about 11:30 P.M." by the Newhall Land and Farming Company's report of March 24.[3][1] The water ran down the canyon to the Santa Clara River at Castaic Junction and west through Piru, Fillmore, Santa Paula and Saticoy, and reached the ocean below Ventura at 5:25 a.m. on March 13, 54 miles from the dam.[3]

The first miles of that path were this valley's. A mile and a half below the dam the flood swept away Powerhouse No. 2 and the homes of its workers. Alan Pollack counts three survivors there: Lillian Curtis, her son Danny, and the utility man Ray Rising. Lillian lost her husband, Lyman, and their daughters, Marjorie and Mazie.[4][5] Lower in the canyon the water killed members of the Ruiz family, who were buried in the family's cemetery, and destroyed the trading post and part of Harry Carey's ranch.[6][7] At Castaic Junction it took the highway and railroad bridges, the Edison company's transformer station and its workers' cottages, a gasoline station whose operator and one of his sons were lost, and an auto camp; the Newhall Land report of March 24 found "not a vestige of any building whatsoever" there but the concrete platform of the old section house.[8] Beyond the junction it overturned the Southern Pacific's track and struck the Edison construction camp at Kemp, by the Los Angeles-Ventura county line, where Pollack counts 84 workers and the night watchman, Ed Locke, among the dead.[9][10] Newhall Land counted 1,720 acres of its ranch totally destroyed.[11] Newhall itself was spared. "The town of Newhall was not harmed in any way," William S. Hart wrote, "but at one time there were 78 bodies in the little shack that had been converted into a morgue": the Masonic hall at Railroad Avenue and Market Street, where volunteers were setting up slabs by 4 a.m. on March 13.[12][13] Hart's ranch home served as a center for relief work.[14] Seven members of the Saugus Community Club were among the dead.[15]

How many died has been counted many times. Ann Stansell, a graduate student at California State University, Northridge, compiled a roster of the victims by name from 2011 to 2014; in his note of March 12, 2014, Leon Worden gave its total as "431 individuals": 306 recovered bodies, 240 of them identified, and 125 missing persons.[16] On January 17, 2018, he revised the figure on the same page: "the number of victims stands at 411," twenty fewer than the original list. "Each of the 20 had been reported missing in 1928, but no claim had been filed." Stansell had found all twenty in the 1930 census. "They survived."[17] This record gives 411, the archive's latest count. The other figures in the archive's sources are listed below.

On March 25, 1928, Hart and other Newhall cowboys set a stone in the Ruiz Cemetery "In memory of those who lost their lives in the Santa Clara flood Mar. 13, 1928."[18] The dam site was registered as California Historical Landmark No. 919 on April 26, 1978, and dedicated by the Santa Clarita Valley Historical Society on May 21; the state's plaque was placed at Power House No. 2 on November 5, 1979.[19][20] On March 12, 2019, the 91st anniversary, S.47 became law, and with it the Saint Francis Dam Disaster National Memorial and National Monument.[21][22]

The disaster has its own literature: Charles F. Outland's Man-Made Disaster: The Story of St. Francis Dam (1963, revised 1977); J. David Rogers's work in The St. Francis Dam Disaster Revisited (1995) and his paper for the American Society of Civil Engineers (2007); Norris Hundley Jr. and Donald C. Jackson's Heavy Ground (2015); and Jon Wilkman's Floodpath (2016).[23][24][25][26] Its primary record includes the transcript of the coroner's inquest and the jury's verdict of April 12, 1928, the Citizens' Restoration Committee's report on death and disability claims of July 15, 1929, and Stansell's roster and thesis.[27][28][29]

Newhall Jr., "Report on St. Francis Dam Flood for The Newhall Land and Farming Company," San Francisco, March 24, 1928, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/nlf-stfrancis.htm. Written eleven days after the flood. The dam was "Completed about two years ago by the City of Los Angeles for the storage of an emergency water supply"; the flood followed "the breaking of the St. Francis dam at the head of the San Francisquito Canyon on or about 11:30 P.M. Monday, March 12th, 1928."
Leon Worden, "William Mulholland, St. Francis Dam Builder," LW2054, photograph #28063 in this archive. See also the person record for William Mulholland, #16432.

Caption to AL3024a, "Dam Under Construction" (photograph, collection of Alan Pollack), as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/al3024a.htm: "At 11:57:30 on the night of March 12, 1928, half of the dam suddenly collapsed." "Floodwaters met the Santa Clara River at Castaic Junction and headed west toward the Pacific Ocean. The communities of Piru, Fillmore, Santa Paula, Saticoy and much of Ventura were leveled before the water, mud and debris completed their 54-mile journey to the ocean at 5:25 a.m. on March 13th." The same time stands in the caption carried on the archive's other photographs of the dam ("At 11:57:30 p.m. on March 12, 1928, the dam failed"), and on the Santa Clarita Valley Historical Society's plaque of 1978 ("At 11:57½ P.M., March 12, 1928").

Alan Pollack, "St. Francis Dam Disaster: Victims and Heroes," Heritage Junction Dispatch, March-April 2008, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/pollack0308victims.htm: "A mile and a half downstream from the dam was a group of homes for workers at Powerhouse No. 2." Of Lillian Curtis and her son: "The mother and son were the family's only survivors." Of Ray Rising: "He was the only other survivor at this powerhouse. The building itself was swept away by the flood, leaving only the floor slab."

J. Timothy Fives, "Memorial to St. Francis Dam," The Newhall Signal and Saugus Enterprise, May 22, 1978, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sg19780522dam.htm: Mrs. Lillian Eilers, "who was sleeping at the family quarters of Powerhouse 2 several miles downstream when the dam broke," "managed to pluck her three-year-old son from the water that swept away the powerhouse but lost her husband and two other children." See also Leon Worden, "'Historic' event with real life, real death," The Signal, February 26, 2003, article #12214 in this archive, on Lyman, Lillian, Marjorie, Mazie and Danny Curtis.

Ruiz Cemetery, place record #2536 in this archive: "Six members of the Ruiz family died when the dam broke on March 12, 1928: the parents, Rosaria and Enrique, and their four children, aged eight to thirty." Leon Worden, "Requiem to a Little Soldier" (the page "Bill Hart and the Little Dam Victim"), The Signal, May 17, 2003, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sg051703.htm, gives more: the Ruiz Cemetery, "where eight members of the prominent Ruiz family had been buried the Sunday before" March 25, 1928. The two counts are not reconciled here.

Photoplay, May 1928, page 6, "As we go to Press / Last Minute News from East and West," reproduced with Leon Worden's notes as LW2271, "Original Ranch House in Photoplay Magazine, 1928," photograph #3149 in this archive (/scvhistory/lw2271.htm). Published weeks after the flood. "Harry Carey ranch at Saugus, Calif., was destroyed by the breaking of the St. Francis Dam." Leon Worden's note on the same page: the ranch house pictured "wasn't lost in the flood"; the Trading Post's "operators died in the disaster." Alan Pollack, "St. Francis Dam Disaster: Victims and Heroes," Heritage Junction Dispatch, March-April 2008, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/pollack0308victims.htm: the flood "destroyed part of the ranch, including a Navajo Trading Post."

A.M. [Almer M.] Newhall and Geo. A. Newhall Jr., "Report on St. Francis Dam Flood for The Newhall Land and Farming Company," San Francisco, March 24, 1928, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/nlf-stfrancis.htm. Written eleven days after the flood. At Castaic Junction (the report's "Castaic"; webmaster's note 4: "Castaic Junction, where State Route 126 meets Interstate 5"): the flood struck "the railroad and highway bridges and the transformer station of the Edison Company," where "everything except two galvanized iron buildings in which the large transformers were housed was carried away," with "the wooden cottages that formerly housed the Edison Company employees"; at "the gasoline station operated by McIntyre and his son ... the father and one of the boys were lost"; at "a large auto camp ... it was reported there were some eight cars whose occupants were undoubtedly lost"; "there is not a vestige of any building whatsoever in that country except the concrete platform of the old section house." See also AL2020, "Castaic Highway Bridge Destroyed by Floodwaters, March 1928," /scvhistory/al2020.htm, and photograph #4177 in this archive (LW2579), "Detail from panoramic photograph of Castaic Junction on March 18, 1928, showing flood damage from the St. Francis Dam."

A.M. [Almer M.] Newhall and Geo. A. Newhall Jr., "Report on St. Francis Dam Flood for The Newhall Land and Farming Company," San Francisco, March 24, 1928, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/nlf-stfrancis.htm. Written eleven days after the flood. "about a quarter of a mile from Castaic, we next come to a point where the S.P. railroad tracks are literally turned upside down"; "Thus the overturned tracks continued for a matter of about a quarter to a half mile."

A.M. [Almer M.] Newhall and Geo. A. Newhall Jr., "Report on St. Francis Dam Flood for The Newhall Land and Farming Company," San Francisco, March 24, 1928, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/nlf-stfrancis.htm. Written eleven days after the flood. "Just west of the Los Angeles-Ventura County Line is the S.P. siding known as \"Kemp\", and the land immediately south of this we had rented to the Southern California Edison Construction Camp for a crew of some 150 to 200 men who were putting in new power lines." Alan Pollack, "St. Francis Dam Disaster: Victims and Heroes," Heritage Junction Dispatch, March-April 2008, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/pollack0308victims.htm: "Just past the Ventura County line along the Santa Clara River was a railroad siding called Kemp"; the night watchman Ed Locke "perished that night, along with 84 of the workers." Pollack's extended timeline of 2014 (/scvhistory/stfrancistimeline_pollack2014.htm) puts the camp "just east of the Los Angeles-Ventura county line." The sources disagree on which side of the line it stood.

A.M. [Almer M.] Newhall and Geo. A. Newhall Jr., "Report on St. Francis Dam Flood for The Newhall Land and Farming Company," San Francisco, March 24, 1928, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/nlf-stfrancis.htm. Written eleven days after the flood. The report's table totals "1720 acres" under "Totally destroyed": irrigated alfalfa land, dry farming land, orange orchard, and the pecan orchard with land to have been planted that year.

William S. Hart to Wyatt Earp, May 8, 1928, as quoted by Truman Rex Fisher, letter to the editor, Los Angeles Times, February 15, 2003, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/lat021503.htm: "The town of Newhall was not harmed in any way but at one time there were 78 bodies in the little shack that had been converted into a morgue."

The caption also calls the building the Hap-A-Lan dance hall. Leon Worden, "Requiem to a Little Soldier" (the page "Bill Hart and the Little Dam Victim"), The Signal, May 17, 2003, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sg051703.htm: "By 4 a.m., volunteers were already starting to fill the Masonic lodge in Newhall, normally a happy and popular dance hall, with improvised slabs for the dead."

Published weeks after the flood. "Bill Hart's new ranch home at Newhall, Calif., escaped in the big dam disaster, being on the very edge of the flood. Leon Worden, "Saugus Community Club Plaque for 7 Members Who Perished in 1928 Dam Disaster," LW2731 (photo gallery, December 27, 2014), as carried on SCVHistory.com, /gif/galleries/lw2731/index.html. It's a grand total of 431 individuals."

editorNotes.heading: Content advisory
editorNotes.note: This record concerns a dam failure and flood in which hundreds of people died, and describes the recovery of bodies and a temporary morgue.

editorNotes.heading: The time of the failure
editorNotes.note: Leon Worden's captions, Alan Pollack's timeline of 2014 and the Historical Society's plaque of 1978 give 11:57:30 p.m. (the plaque, "11:57½ P.M."); the SCVHistory.com timeline gives 11:57 p.m. The Newhall Land and Farming Company's report, written March 24, 1928, says "on or about 11:30 P.M." Pollack's timeline ties 11:57:30 to a sharp drop in voltage noted at the Bureau of Water Works and Supply's receiving stations in Los Angeles and at Powerhouse No. 1. Both times are kept.

editorNotes.heading: The number of dead in the sources
editorNotes.note: The sources in this archive give these figures for the dead, each as its source states it. 1928: the Newhall Land and Farming Company's report of March 24, "probably almost five hundred" (/scvhistory/nlf-stfrancis.htm); newspaper headlines of March 13 and 14, from "200 Dead" (The Detroit News, AL2034) to "FLOOD DEATHS NEAR 1000" (Chicago Daily Tribune, AL2048). A Los Angeles Times negative sleeve at UCLA, quoted on LW2715: "more than 600 residents plus an unknown number of itinerant farm workers", and "Up to March 18, 273 bodies had been recovered." 1978: The Newhall Signal, "more than 400 persons"; Leon Worden's caption to the same page, "nearly 450 lives" (/scvhistory/sg19780522dam.htm); the Historical Society's plaque, "At least 425 lives"; the state's description of Landmark No. 919, "Over 450 lives" (HS7801). Later: the SCVHistory.com timeline, "more than 450"; Leon Worden's Concise History, "more than 450 dead bodies" (/scvhistory/lwhist.htm); Paul H. Rippens, 1998, "over 450 lives"; Leon Worden, 2003, "An estimated 450 people", with his later note "Estimate as of 2019: 411 people" (/scvhistory/sg051703.htm); J. David Rogers, 2007, "more than 432 people"; Alan Pollack, 2008, "between 450 and 600"; Pollack, 2016, "some 431" and "over 400" (/scvhistory/pollack0716stfrancis.htm); Ann Stansell's roster, 2014, 431; Leon Worden's revision of it, 2018, 411. The archive's photograph captions carry three versions of one sentence: "An estimated 470 people" (the ES1928 photographs), "An estimated 431 people" (older captions) and "An estimated 411 people" (current ones).

researchLeads: Stansell's current list (annstansell_damvictims011718.pdf) was not read: the Reggie drive was not mounted and the local index holds HTML only. Her 2014 table (431 names) has a 'General Area' column; counted from the HTML on 5 October 2026: Edison - Kemp Camp 85; Unknown - Unidentified 66; BP&L - PP2 Community 63; Unavailable - No Claim 39; San Francisquito Canyon 36; Bardsdale 32; Newhall Ranch Land 24; Fillmore 18; SP - Castaic Junction 17; Santa Paula 16; BWWS - PP2 Community 10; Castaic Junction 9; Piru 7; Newhall 5; Saugus 2; Edison - Castaic Junction 2. Which twenty the 2018 revision removed is not stated on the page. Reading the PDF would give a valley count on the archive's current figure.

Powerhouse No. 2: Pollack 2008 counts three survivors; Pollack's 2014 timeline says the flood 'claims the lives of 64 of the 67 workmen and their family members who lived nearby'; Stansell's 2014 table puts 73 in the PP2 community (63 BP&L, 10 BWWS). Not reconciled; the body gives only Pollack 2008's survivors.

Pollack's 2014 extended timeline gives metric conversions in parentheses ('1-1/2 miles (2.4 km)', '18 mph (29 km/h)'), the style of an encyclopedia article. It may share text with an outside compilation; its figures not found elsewhere in the archive (64 of 67; wave heights) are treated here as leads, and the body does not rest on it except for the Kemp location disagreement.
Ruiz family: six killed (Ruiz Cemetery record #2536; Pollack 2014) against eight Ruiz buried on March 18, 1928 (Leon Worden 2003, sg051703). HB1901 and the hub's 'Ruiz Family x7' are further leads.

The Newhall morgue: Leon's captions (LW2715, FR2801) and his 2003 column treat the Masonic hall and the Hap-A-Lan dance hall as one building. The Reynolds dossier (inventory/review/jerry-reynolds-sources.md, H3 and RX1) marks Reynolds's 'Hap-A-Lan dance hall' as contradicted by the Newhall Signal of 1928 ('Masonic lodge'). If they are one building, the dossier verdict is wrong on that point. The body names only the Masonic hall at Railroad Avenue and Market Street, which both accounts support.

Bodies at the Newhall morgue: Hart (May 8, 1928) 78 'at one time'; LW2715 'At least 78'; FR2801 'some 70 bodies'. The Newhall Signal of March 29 and April 5, 1928, quoted in sg051703, were not located as scans in the mirror for this draft.

Harry Carey's Navajo employees: Photoplay May 1928, 'Sixty-four Navajo Indians, employed at the trading post, had left for their reservation'; LW2135, 'they went away that morning'; Pollack 2008, citing Harry Carey Jr., a month before. Not in the body.

The Saugus Community Clubhouse, 23027 Drayton St., 'was utilized as an emergency shelter (per Ann Stansell 2014 PC) and possibly as a morgue (per Don Ray 2014 PC)' (LW2731). Personal communications only; not in the body.

Edison Saugus substation: HS7067 quotes Wilkman 2016:94, 97 and Hundley & Jackson 2015:144 on the night crew and the destroyed cottages. The books are not in the archive; the body rests on the Newhall Land report instead.

Construction dates and dimensions disagree across the captions (August 1924 start in the captions against 'December 1: Construction work begins (source: L.A. Times, 7-25-1926)' in the timeline; '600-foot-long, 185-foot-high' against '700-foot-long, 205-foot-high'). The body gives neither.
